title: Mapping Healthcare Across the United States
text:
I wanted to explore healthcare in the United States from two different perspectives. First, I looked at where Mayo Clinic’s three major campuses are located. Then, I explored health insurance coverage across the country to get a better understanding of differences in healthcare access between states!
The maps below use both categorical and numeric data to show these patterns. The interactive maps also let you explore individual states and learn more about the information behind each visualization.

title: Mapping Healthcare Across the United States
text:
1. Mayo Clinic’s Geographic Presence
Mayo Clinic has three major campus locations in the United States: Arizona, Florida, and Minnesota. I wanted to see how these campuses are spread across the country and highlight the states where they are located.

Prepare the Mayo Clinic Data


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(maps)
library(leaflet)
library(sf)
library(tidycensus)

# Mayo Clinic campus data
mayo_data <- tibble(
  state_name = c("arizona", "florida", "minnesota"),
  mayo_campus = c(1, 1, 1)
)

# Locations of the three major campuses
mayo_locations <- tibble(
  location = c(
    "Mayo Clinic Arizona",
    "Mayo Clinic Florida",
    "Mayo Clinic Rochester"
  ),
  state = c("Arizona", "Florida", "Minnesota"),
  longitude = c(-112.0740, -81.6557, -92.4630),
  latitude = c(33.4484, 30.3322, 44.0121)
)

# State map data
us_states <- map_data("state")

# Join Mayo Clinic data with state map data
mayo_states <- us_states |>
  left_join(mayo_data, by = c("region" = "state_name")) |>
  mutate(mayo_campus = replace_na(mayo_campus, 0))

# Interactive state map data
states <- read_sf(
  "https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/json/us-states.geojson"
) |>
  filter(!name %in% c("Alaska", "Hawaii", "District of Columbia"))

states_mayo <- states |>
  mutate(state_name = str_to_lower(name)) |>
  left_join(mayo_data, by = "state_name") |>
  mutate(mayo_campus = replace_na(mayo_campus, 0))




Static Map: Major Campus Locations
This map highlights the three states where Mayo Clinic has major campuses. The states are shaded in maroon, and the dots represent the approximate locations of each campus. The campuses are spread across different regions of the country, with Rochester, Minnesota, being home to Mayo Clinic’s original campus.


Show code
ggplot(mayo_states, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(
    aes(fill = factor(mayo_campus)),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = mayo_locations,
    aes(x = longitude, y = latitude),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "maroon",
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("0" = "pink", "1" = "maroon"),
    labels = c("No major campus", "Major campus"),
    name = "Mayo Clinic presence"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Mayo Clinic's Major Campus Locations",
    subtitle = "Dots represent the approximate locations of the three major campuses",
    caption = "Source: Mayo Clinic. Campus dots use approximate city-center coordinates."
  ) +
  coord_map() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )











Interactive Map: Explore Mayo Clinic’s Locations
This interactive map provides another way to explore Mayo Clinic’s presence across the United States. States with a major Mayo Clinic campus are highlighted in maroon, while the remaining states are shown in pink. You can hover over states to see whether they have a major campus and click on the markers to learn which campus is located there.


Show code
mayo_colors <- colorFactor(
  palette = c("pink", "maroon"),
  domain = c(0, 1)
)

states_mayo <- states_mayo |>
  mutate(
    labels = paste0(
      name,
      ifelse(
        mayo_campus == 1,
        ": Has a major Mayo Clinic campus",
        ": No major campus"
      )
    )
  )

leaflet(states_mayo) |>
  setView(lng = -96, lat = 37.8, zoom = 4) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~mayo_colors(mayo_campus),
    weight = 2,
    opacity = 1,
    color = "white",
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
      weight = 5,
      color = "darkgray",
      fillOpacity = 0.7,
      bringToFront = TRUE
    ),
    label = ~labels
  ) |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    data = mayo_locations,
    lat = ~latitude,
    lng = ~longitude,
    popup = ~paste0("<b>", location, "</b><br>", state),
    label = ~location,
    radius = 6,
    color = "maroon",
    fillColor = "pink",
    fillOpacity = 0.9
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = mayo_colors,
    values = ~mayo_campus,
    title = "Mayo Clinic presence",
    labels = c("No major campus", "Major campus"),
    position = "bottomright"
  )

title: Mapping Healthcare Across the United States
section: 2. Health Insurance Coverage Across the United States
text:
2. Health Insurance Coverage Across the United States
I also wanted to explore differences in health insurance coverage across the country. I used data from the American Community Survey to look at the percentage of people in each state who do not have health insurance. This provides another perspective on healthcare access and helps show how coverage varies geographically.

Prepare the Health Insurance Data


Show code
# Get state-level uninsured rates from the 2024 ACS
key <-"828101d14a9c6f7acd91b9fc7aac72a4037dc608"
uninsured_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "state",
  variables = c(uninsured_rate = "S2701_C05_001"),
  year = 2024,
  survey = "acs1"
) |>
  select(NAME, estimate, moe) |>
  rename(
    state_name = NAME,
    uninsured_rate = estimate,
    margin_of_error = moe
  ) |>
  mutate(state_name = str_to_lower(state_name))

# Join uninsured data with the static state map
uninsured_states <- us_states |>
  left_join(
    uninsured_data,
    by = c("region" = "state_name")
  )

# Join uninsured data with the interactive state map
states_uninsured <- states |>
  mutate(state_name = str_to_lower(name)) |>
  left_join(
    uninsured_data,
    by = "state_name"
  )




Static Map: Uninsured Rates by State
This map shows the percentage of the population without health insurance in each state in 2024. States with higher uninsured rates are shaded in darker maroon, while states with lower rates are lighter pink. This makes it easier to compare states and identify geographic patterns in health insurance coverage.


Show code
ggplot(
  uninsured_states,
  aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)
) +
  geom_polygon(
    aes(fill = uninsured_rate),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "pink",
    high = "maroon",
    name = "Uninsured rate (%)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Uninsured Rates Across the United States",
    subtitle = "Percentage of the population without health insurance, 2024",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2024 American Community Survey, Table S2701."
  ) +
  coord_map() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )











Interactive Map: Explore Uninsured Rates
This interactive map allows you to explore uninsured rates state by state. States with higher uninsured rates appear darker, while states with lower rates appear lighter. You can hover over each state to see its estimated uninsured percentage and click on it for additional information, including the margin of error.


Show code
uninsured_colors <- colorNumeric(
  palette = c("pink", "maroon"),
  domain = states_uninsured$uninsured_rate
)

states_uninsured <- states_uninsured |>
  mutate(
    labels = paste0(
      name,
      ": ",
      round(uninsured_rate, 1),
      "% uninsured"
    ),
    popups = paste0(
      "<b>", name, "</b><br>",
      "Uninsured rate: ",
      round(uninsured_rate, 1), "%<br>",
      "Margin of error: ±",
      round(margin_of_error, 1),
      " percentage points"
    )
  )

leaflet(states_uninsured) |>
  setView(lng = -96, lat = 37.8, zoom = 4) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~uninsured_colors(uninsured_rate),
    weight = 2,
    opacity = 1,
    color = "white",
    fillOpacity = 0.75,
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
      weight = 5,
      color = "darkgray",
      fillOpacity = 0.85,
      bringToFront = TRUE
    ),
    label = ~labels,
    popup = ~popups
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = uninsured_colors,
    values = ~uninsured_rate,
    title = "Uninsured rate (%)",
    position = "bottomright"
  )

What is igraph?
igraph is an R package used to create, visualize, and analyze networks.
It allows you to study relationships between observations instead of looking at each data point individually!

Discovering patterns in networks
Identifying important connections in data

Understanding Network Structure

Nodes (vertices): Represent individual objects
Edges: Represent relationships or connections

Networks can be:

Undirected: Connections go both ways
Directed: Connections have a specific direction

I wanted to explore where these campuses are located and get a better understanding of Mayo Clinic’s geographic presence across the country. The maps below show the locations of the three major campuses and allow you to explore which states have a major Mayo Clinic campus.

library(tidyverse)

mayo_states <- us_states |>
  left_join(mayo_data, by = c("region" = "state_name")) |>

mayo_locations <- tibble(

  longitude = c(-112.0740, -81.6557, -92.4630),

title: How Does Thor’s Dialogue Change in Thor: Ragnarok?
text:
Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)

ragnarok <- read_csv("miniproject1/ragnarok.csv")

title: How Does Thor’s Dialogue Change in Thor: Ragnarok?
text:
Introduction
Thor: Ragnarok is full of action, family drama, and funny conversations. I wanted to see whether Thor’s dialogue changes as the movie goes on. Does he ask more questions or use more exclamations at certain points? Does the length of his dialogue change? I also wanted to see which words he uses most often and whether his language becomes more positive or negative. To explore this, I used a dataset of dialogue from the movie. I treated the rows as being in the same order as the movie and divided Thor’s lines into three sections: beginning, middle, and end. This is an approximate division, not an exact division into scenes.

title: How Does Thor’s Dialogue Change in Thor: Ragnarok?
text:
Getting the dialogue ready
First, I kept the rows containing Thor’s dialogue and cleaned up the text to make it easier to analyze. I used str_to_lower() to make the text lowercase, str_replace_all() to remove punctuation, and str_length() to measure the length of each line. I also divided Thor’s dialogue into three sections: beginning, middle, and end.


Show code
thor <- ragnarok |>
  filter(str_detect(str_to_lower(character), "thor")) |>
  mutate(
    clean_line = str_replace_all(str_to_lower(line), "[^a-z ]", " "),
    line_length = str_length(line),
    line_number = row_number(),
    section = ifelse(line_number <= n()/3, "Beginning",
              ifelse(line_number <= 2*n()/3, "Middle", "End"))
  )

title: How Does Thor’s Dialogue Change in Thor: Ragnarok?
text:
1. Does Thor’s dialogue get longer?
I started by checking whether the length of Thor’s lines changes across the movie. A longer line does not necessarily mean a more important line, but it is one simple way to compare how much he says at different points.


Show code
line_lengths <- thor |>
  group_by(section) |>
  summarise(average_length = mean(line_length))

line_lengths |>
  ggplot(aes(x = section, y = average_length)) +
  geom_col(fill = "pink", color = "gray") +
  labs(title = "How long are Thor's lines?",
       x = "Part of movie", y = "Average characters per line") +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 1: Average number of characters in Thor’s dialogue lines by section.





The chart compares the average length of Thor’s lines in each section. The average line lengths are 44.8, 49.9, 50.8 characters for beginning, middle, and end, respectively. The section with the tallest bar has the longest lines on average. This measures line length, not how emotional or meaningful the dialogue is.

title: How Does Thor’s Dialogue Change in Thor: Ragnarok?
section: 2. How does Thor’s speaking style change?
text:
2. How does Thor’s speaking style change?
Next, I wanted to see how Thor’s speaking style changes throughout the movie. I looked at how often he asks questions, uses exclamation marks, and uses longer words. I used str_detect() with three different regular expressions to identify these patterns. The regular expression \\? looks for question marks, ! looks for exclamation marks, and \\b[a-z]{8,}\\b looks for words containing eight or more letters. This helped me compare different patterns in Thor’s dialogue without focusing on specific words.


Show code
themes <- thor |>
  mutate(
    questions = str_detect(line, "\\?"),
    exclamations = str_detect(line, "!"),
    long_words = str_detect(clean_line, "\\b[a-z]{8,}\\b")
  ) |>
  group_by(section) |>
  summarise(
    Questions = sum(questions),
    Exclamations = sum(exclamations),
    Long_Words = sum(long_words)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Questions, Exclamations, Long_Words),
    names_to = "theme",
    values_to = "lines"
  )




Show code
themes |>
  ggplot(aes(x = section, y = lines, fill = theme)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Questions" = "pink",
    "Exclamations" = "gray",
    "Long_Words" = "maroon"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "How does Thor's speaking style change?",
    x = "Part of movie",
    y = "Number of lines",
    fill = "Dialogue pattern"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 2: Number of Thor’s lines containing questions, exclamations, or long words in each section.





This chart lets me compare how Thor’s speaking style changes throughout the movie. I wanted to see whether he asks more questions, uses more exclamation marks, or uses longer words in different sections. These patterns might help show changes in how he communicates. However, just because Thor uses more exclamation marks or longer words does not necessarily mean he is more emotional or serious. The chart only shows how often these patterns appear in his dialogue.

title: How Does Thor’s Dialogue Change in Thor: Ragnarok?
section: 3. Which words does Thor use most?

title: How Does Thor’s Dialogue Change in Thor: Ragnarok?
section: 4. Does Thor’s language become more positive or negative?
text:
4. Does Thor’s language become more positive or negative?
For my second text-analysis application, I used Bing sentiment analysis. The Bing list labels certain words as positive or negative. I compared the number of positive and negative words in each section.


Show code
sentiment_words <- words |>
  inner_join(get_sentiments("bing"), by = "word") |>
  count(section, sentiment)




Show code
sentiment_words |>
  ggplot(aes(x = section, y = n, fill = sentiment)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("positive" = "maroon",
                             "negative" = "gray")) +
  labs(title = "Positive and negative words across the movie",
       x = "Part of movie", y = "Number of sentiment words",
       fill = "Sentiment") +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 4: Counts of words classified as positive or negative by the Bing sentiment lexicon, across three sections of Thor’s dialogue.





This plot compares positive and negative word counts. It can help identify changes in the language Thor uses, but it cannot tell us exactly how Thor feels. For example, a character might use a negative word while making a joke. Since I divided Thor’s lines into three nearly equal groups, the sections have similar numbers of lines, but not necessarily the same number of words.

title: How Does Thor’s Dialogue Change in Thor: Ragnarok?
text:
Conclusion
By looking at Thor’s dialogue in different ways, I can see how text analysis helps us ask questions about a movie beyond its plot. Line lengths show how much Thor says at a time, regular expressions help track topics like family and fighting, word counts show repeated language, and sentiment analysis compares positive and negative words. The biggest limitation is that these tools cannot understand sarcasm, context, or the meaning of a whole scene. Even so, these simple methods offer a useful starting point for exploring how Thor’s dialogue changes during Ragnarok.
